title: The man born blind. Part 4
scripture_text: ‘’As he went along, he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” “Neither this man nor his parents sinned,”said Jesus, “but this happened so that the works of God might be displayed in him. As long as it is day, we must do the works of him who sent me. Night is coming, when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” After saying this, he spit on the ground, made some mud with the saliva, and put it on the man’s eyes. “Go,” he told him, “wash in the Pool of Siloam” (this word means “Sent”). So the man went and washed, and came home seeing.’’
devotional:
The healing of the blind man.

A few initial observations.

The New Testament records more accounts of Jesus restoring sight than any other miracle (Mk. 18:22-26; 10:46-52; Mt. 9:27-31; 12:22-23; 21:14; Mk. 8:22-26; Jn. 9:1-41). This predicted Messianic activity (Isa. 29:18; 35:5; 42:7) it became somewhat of a hallmark of His ministry.

Jesus never healed two blind people in the same way, he treated people as individuals. It is so easy when ministering to others to try and establish some kind of formula, or a ‘one size fits all’ approach, but in doing this we cease to treat people as people and more like objects.

It is quite striking that the only reference to healing of blindness in the Bible other than in Jesus' ministry, is the case of Paul, it was Jesus who both blinded and restored him. So Jesus' healing of the blind stands out as a major sign of his identity and the significance of his coming.

Look at what Jesus did here.

Firstly Jesus took the initiative. This blind man did not ask Jesus to heal him; Jesus saw his need and responded. Secondly, the method used by Jesus in the healing of the blind man might sound a little unusual to us, but would have been common practice in ancient times. The application of herbs and poultices to infected areas of the body was widely accepted as the proper application of their limited medical science. Certainly, the poultice had no intrinsic healing power. John emphasizes the use of the mud mentioning it in 9:6, 11, 14, 15. There has been much debate about why Jesus did this. Some commentators believe that there is allusion to the biblical picture of God as a potter and human beings as clay (for example, Job 10:9; Is 45:9; 64:8; Jer 18:6; Rom 9:2,) but this is unlikely because the picture of the potter in the bible is primarily a picture of someone who is in the process of judging or disciplining his people while they are still on the earth. Jesus did not need to put the mud on this blind man in order to heal him, but he chose to do so.

I wonder could I make a suggestion as to a ‘possible’ reason why Jesus chose to use this method at this time. To teach his disciples a very important lesson. Jesus knew that as he spat on the ground and made the mud, he was breaking the oral traditions on the elders and the expectations of the religious leaders.

Rabbinic teaching perverted the Old Testament into a straight-jacket catalogue of rules. In healing this man on the Sabbath, Jesus violated four of their rules: ploughing (spittle rolling on the dirt), kneading (making the clay), anointing (putting clay on the man's eyes), and of course healing (illegal unless a life-threatening emergency). Jesus hated the way religion elevated ritual observance over human need, and never hesitated to break its rules. Jesus was saying, if you are frightened of men, and feel that you must conform to their rules and traditions, and then you will not show love and compassion to those who need it.

Thirdly sent to Siloam, a parable of his life of faith.

The healing was not effected until the man obeyed Jesus' command: Go wash in the Pool of Siloam (9:7). Why didn't Jesus just heal him on the spot, as he did with others? Why send a blind man in particular, on such a journey? There must be something involved here that contributes to the revealing of God's work.

What Jesus did was to demand an act of faith by the man being healed. The man could have simply said, "This is ridiculous," wiped the dirt from his eyes, and gone home blind. Instead, he had to walk a distance through one of the busiest and most crowded streets of the city to the pool. He would then have to wash his eyes at the pool while others watched. For a blind man, this would be very difficult. He would have to ask for directions and for help, and he might easily fall into some of the crevices alongside the road on the way down. It was difficult, but necessary. For the man needed to know that to become a man of vision didn’t mean that all his problems were solved. In going to the pool of Siloam, the blind man learnt that Jesus could be trusted and obeyed.

John tells us that that the word Siloam means sent. Throughout this gospel Jesus is referred to as the one whom God has sent 51 times. To follow the sent one will restore our vision, but it will not remove the pain and stress of life. For this man to put his faith in Jesus, he would face opposition and obstacles, as we shall see in the rest of the chapter.

The spiritual significance of the miracle.

This miracle was a signpost of Jesus’, redeeming work. We are all spiritually blind and there’s nothing that we can do to remove that blindness. Only Jesus has the ability to give spiritual vision which will help us to see ourselves and the world in which we live, as we really are.
prayer: Father thank you that Jesus treated every blind man that he healed differently.
